description: We are a team of passionate astronomers, musicians and nature lovers, aiming to sonify the Earth for educational—as well as playfully scientific—purposes. We belive in sound and its power !
summary:
We wanted to raise awareness and help people about the changes in our planet and its natural beauty, so we have created an "Earth Jukebox" which is a web repository app that turns real NASA Earth data into sound, in real time. Users explore one interactive globe with seven layers: ocean currents, sea temperature, salinity, plankton, forests, fauna and algae. As they move a point across the globe, the app reads the measured value at that spot and maps it to pitch, rhythm and timbre, choosing the sound that best fits each phenomenon (wooden percussion for forests, for example). Notes follow a pentatonic scale, so the result stays musical.

It addresses the challenge by making visual-only data accessible to everyone. A dedicated Accessibility section offers profiles for people who can’t hear (sound captions, a colored shape for every note, vibration) and for people who can’t see (a veil that hides the globe so it is explored by ear, a guide sound, spoken descriptions, screen-reader support, keyboard control).

It is also educational: guided tours, missions, badges and information with sources teach how the planet works as people play and navigate. It also runs in VR.
Sound reveals patterns the eye misses. 

We could develop by adding original recordings, growing it into a musical library of Earth’s sounds and beyond !
details:
Earth Jukebox aloud users to pick in between seven layers: ocean currents, sea temperature, salinity, plankton (ocean colour from NASA PACE), forests (canopy height from NASA GEDI), fauna (animal migrations) and algae. By clicking or moving a point on the globe the app reads the value at that point, over time, and converts it into a signal from 0 to 100, where 50 is the usual value for that place. That signal drives pitch, rhythm and timbre. Each layer has its own instruments: forests use only wooden percussion, chosen by forest type, currents and temperature use kalimba, vibraphone or crystal tones depending on latitude, salinity uses a glass harmonica and ocean colour a flute. Notes follow a pentatonic scale, so the result stays musical. The app also includes a solar-system menu (each body plays a note tied to its orbital period), guided tours with sources, and a missions game with XP and downloadable badges. The app uses real data from NASA satellites and visualizations (ECCO2, GEDI, PACE, SVS and others). Where a value is an estimate derived from image colours, the app labels it as such.

Researchers and students can explore how the data change over time, comparing past data in this way helps spot trends that can inform future projections.

People learn as they play: every layer, tour stop and mission comes with information and links to the original NASA sources, so users can get deeper information's.

Users could hear scales, notes and instruments, and learn how each sound is tied to the place and the phenomenon.

It makes visual-only climate data accessible to blind, low-vision, and deaf or hard-of-hearing people, through a dedicated Accessibility section.

A veil that hides the globe, a continuous guide sound (pitch tells latitude, stereo tells longitude), spoken descriptions, screen-reader announcements and full keyboard control, raises awareness towards those who haven't that disability.

For people who can’t hear: live sound captions, a coloured shape for every note, vibration and optional light flashes (limited to three per second).

For low vision: high contrast, larger text and reduced animation.

It is free, works in the browser with no account, and progress stays on the user’s device.

We want climate and ocean science to be something everyone can explore and feel, not only something to look at. Listening can reveal patterns the eye misses and builds an emotional link with the planet. Sighted people can also use the veil to experience the data the way blind users do. The project has enormous potential for expansion: more datasets and layers, original recordings and a growing musical library of Earth’s sounds. Our final goal is a live multisensory exhibition, holographic or analogue, where visitors can see, hear and feel the planet’s data together.

The app does not make predictions itself. It lets researchers and students look at past data and see trends, so I wrote “help spot trends that can inform future projections” to keep it accurate.

We consider accessibility first: blind, low-vision, deaf and light-sensitive users, plus reduced motion, keyboard-only use and high contrast. Scientific honesty: some values are estimates derived from the colours of NASA images, and the app labels them as such. The mapping from data to sound and the choice of instruments are artistic choices, not measurements, and the app says so. Musicality versus fidelity: a direct data-to-sound conversion produces noise, so we used scales and instruments chosen for each context. Privacy and simplicity: no accounts or server, and progress is saved only on the device.

A Multisensory immersion experience, driven by stunning visual and sound.

In Sound We Believe, And it's Power !
